# Passenger Boarding (Enplanement) and All-Cargo Data for U.S. Airports

Passenger boarding (enplanement) and all-cargo data is extracted from the FAA's Air Carrier Activity database. This database supports the FAA's airport categories for use in apportionment formula calculations under the [Airport Improvement Program (AIP)](https://www.faa.gov/airports/aip) and [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act programs](https://www.faa.gov/iija).  
[More about the collection and use of passenger and all-cargo data »](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/passenger/collection)

Passenger boarding and all-cargo data is collected for a full calendar year and is used in calculating airport categories and entitlements for the next full fiscal year (i.e., Calendar Year 2025 data determines Fiscal Year 2027 category and funds).

*   **Preliminary**Calendar Year 2025 enplanement and all-cargo data will be available in June 2026.
    *   Any major discrepancies or have questions concerning preliminary all-cargo data or enplanements should promptly be directed to Mr. Luis Loarte at [Luis.Loarte@faa.gov](mailto:Luis.Loarte@faa.gov?subject=Question%20about%20all-cargo%20data%20and%20enplanements) or Mrs. Christina Nutting at [Christina.Nutting@faa.gov](mailto:Christina.Nutting@faa.gov?subject=Question%20about%20all-cargo%20data%20and%20enplanements) by August 14, 2026.

*   **Final**Calendar Year 2025 enplanement and all-cargo data will become available in late August 2026.

Airports can view their individual CY 2025 enplanement report on our [Airports External Portal (AEP)](https://aep.airports.faa.gov/Home.aspx). Please select "Enplanement Public Report and Form" on the AEP site.

See Abbreviations for an explanation of the abbreviations used in the enplanements and cargo files column headings.

## Abbreviations

*   CY = Calendar Year (January 1 through December 31)
*   RO = [FAA Regional Office](https://www.faa.gov/about/office_org/headquarters_offices/arp/offices/regional_offices)
*   ST = Abbreviation for U.S. State or Territory
*   Locid = Location Identifier for a specific airport
*   S/L = Service Level - These are [Airport Categories](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/categories) (P = Primary, CS = Commercial Service, GA = General Aviation).
*   Hub = Hub Size and applies to Commercial Service [Airport Categories](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/categories) (L = Large, M = Medium, S = Small, N = Nonhub Primary, and None = All airports but Primary) based on total CY enplanements.

# Passenger Boarding (Enplanement) and All-Cargo Data for U.S. Airports

Passenger boarding (enplanement) and all-cargo data is extracted from the FAA's Air Carrier Activity database. This database supports the FAA's airport categories for use in apportionment formula calculations under the [Airport Improvement Program (AIP)](https://www.faa.gov/airports/aip) and [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act programs](https://www.faa.gov/iija).  
[More about the collection and use of passenger and all-cargo data »](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/passenger/collection)

Passenger boarding and all-cargo data is collected for a full calendar year and is used in calculating airport categories and entitlements for the next full fiscal year (i.e., Calendar Year 2025 data determines Fiscal Year 2027 category and funds).

*   **Preliminary**Calendar Year 2025 enplanement and all-cargo data will be available in June 2026.
    *   Any major discrepancies or have questions concerning preliminary all-cargo data or enplanements should promptly be directed to Mr. Luis Loarte at [Luis.Loarte@faa.gov](mailto:Luis.Loarte@faa.gov?subject=Question%20about%20all-cargo%20data%20and%20enplanements) or Mrs. Christina Nutting at [Christina.Nutting@faa.gov](mailto:Christina.Nutting@faa.gov?subject=Question%20about%20all-cargo%20data%20and%20enplanements) by August 14, 2026.

*   **Final**Calendar Year 2025 enplanement and all-cargo data will become available in late August 2026.

Airports can view their individual CY 2025 enplanement report on our [Airports External Portal (AEP)](https://aep.airports.faa.gov/Home.aspx). Please select "Enplanement Public Report and Form" on the AEP site.

See Abbreviations for an explanation of the abbreviations used in the enplanements and cargo files column headings.

# 2014 World’s Busiest Airports- Release Date March 26,2015

April 14, 2015

[Business](https://dilemma-x.net/category/business/), [Did you know?](https://dilemma-x.net/category/did-you-know/), [International](https://dilemma-x.net/category/international/)

**2014 World Airport Traffic and Rankings**  
**Release Date March 26, 2015**

**See update: Release Date: April 04, 2016**

> [2015 World’s Busiest Airports- Release Date: April 04, 2016](https://dilemma-x.net/2016/04/06/2015-worlds-busiest-airports-release-date-april-04-2016/)

[![Image 2: Denver International Airport](https://dilemma-x.net/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/denver-international-airport.jpg?w=540&h=317)](https://dilemma-x.net/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/denver-international-airport.jpg)

Airports Council International (ACI)

MONTREAL – Based on reports from 1,095 airports worldwide, ACI’s preliminary passenger traffic results for 2014 show that the top four ranked positions with respect to the world’s busiest airports in overall passenger traffic have not changed as compared to 2013.

Chicago-O’Hare (-0.2%) has become the world’s busiest airport for aircraft movements following a drop in movements at the 2nd ranked Atlanta (-4.7%) in 2014. Los Angeles (+1.7%) and Dallas/Fort Worth (+0.3%) maintain the 3rd and 4th ranked position respectively. Beijing (+2.5%) moves ahead of Denver (-2.9%).

Atlanta (+1.9%) continues to be the world’s busiest airport with over 96 million passengers in 2014. While Beijing (+2.9%) was expected to close the gap, it no longer has double digit-growth as in previous years, placing it in 2nd position. London-Heathrow (+1.4%) remains in 3rd while Tokyo-Haneda (+5.7%) preserves 4th position. However, Los Angeles (+6%) and Dubai (+6.1%) have moved ahead of Chicago-O’Hare (+4.6%), occupying the 5th and 6th rank respectively.

Although Dubai is the 6th busiest airport in the world in overall passenger traffic, it has actually become the world’s busiest in terms of international passenger traffic ahead of London-Heathrow in 2014. Dubai was just shy of reaching the 70 million international passenger mark by the end of 2014.

Istanbul (+10.7%) remains one of the fastest growing airports among the world’s top 20 airports for passenger traffic, moving from 18th to 13th rank ahead of Amsterdam (+4.6%).

The world’s largest air cargo hub continues to be Hong Kong (+6%). Memphis (+2.9%) is in 2nd followed by Shanghai (+8.6%) and Incheon (+3.8%) in 3rd and 4th rank respectively. Anchorage (+3%) moves up ahead of Dubai (-3.1%) to the 5th position.

ACI World’s Economics Director Rafael Echevarne commented: “The airport that continued to make its mark in 2014 was Dubai International. The airport has solidified its status as the world’s major international connecting hub. Dubai is the fulcrum that connects long-haul international flights from east and west, north and south. That being said, it’s sister airport, Dubai World Central, under the same Dubai Airports organization, is poised to surpass these feats by becoming the world’s largest global gateway with capacity of more than 160 million passengers per year and a multi-modal logistics hub for 12 million tonnes of air cargo. Since the commencement of its operations, the airport has already moved up to the 29th busiest air cargo airport in the world handling almost 760,000 metric tonnes of cargo in 2014. With its astonishing capacity and growth, aviation’s nucleus certainly has moved eastward.”

# 2014 World’s Busiest Airports- Release Date March 26,2015

April 14, 2015

[Business](https://dilemma-x.net/category/business/), [Did you know?](https://dilemma-x.net/category/did-you-know/), [International](https://dilemma-x.net/category/international/)

**2014 World Airport Traffic and Rankings**  
**Release Date March 26, 2015**

**See update: Release Date: April 04, 2016**

> [2015 World’s Busiest Airports- Release Date: April 04, 2016](https://dilemma-x.net/2016/04/06/2015-worlds-busiest-airports-release-date-april-04-2016/)

[![Image 2: Denver International Airport](https://dilemma-x.net/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/denver-international-airport.jpg?w=540&h=317)](https://dilemma-x.net/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/denver-international-airport.jpg)

Airports Council International (ACI)

MONTREAL – Based on reports from 1,095 airports worldwide, ACI’s preliminary passenger traffic results for 2014 show that the top four ranked positions with respect to the world’s busiest airports in overall passenger traffic have not changed as compared to 2013.

Chicago-O’Hare (-0.2%) has become the world’s busiest airport for aircraft movements following a drop in movements at the 2nd ranked Atlanta (-4.7%) in 2014. Los Angeles (+1.7%) and Dallas/Fort Worth (+0.3%) maintain the 3rd and 4th ranked position respectively. Beijing (+2.5%) moves ahead of Denver (-2.9%).

Atlanta (+1.9%) continues to be the world’s busiest airport with over 96 million passengers in 2014. While Beijing (+2.9%) was expected to close the gap, it no longer has double digit-growth as in previous years, placing it in 2nd position. London-Heathrow (+1.4%) remains in 3rd while Tokyo-Haneda (+5.7%) preserves 4th position. However, Los Angeles (+6%) and Dubai (+6.1%) have moved ahead of Chicago-O’Hare (+4.6%), occupying the 5th and 6th rank respectively.

Although Dubai is the 6th busiest airport in the world in overall passenger traffic, it has actually become the world’s busiest in terms of international passenger traffic ahead of London-Heathrow in 2014. Dubai was just shy of reaching the 70 million international passenger mark by the end of 2014.

Istanbul (+10.7%) remains one of the fastest growing airports among the world’s top 20 airports for passenger traffic, moving from 18th to 13th rank ahead of Amsterdam (+4.6%).

The world’s largest air cargo hub continues to be Hong Kong (+6%). Memphis (+2.9%) is in 2nd followed by Shanghai (+8.6%) and Incheon (+3.8%) in 3rd and 4th rank respectively. Anchorage (+3%) moves up ahead of Dubai (-3.1%) to the 5th position.

ACI World’s Economics Director Rafael Echevarne commented: “The airport that continued to make its mark in 2014 was Dubai International. The airport has solidified its status as the world’s major international connecting hub. Dubai is the fulcrum that connects long-haul international flights from east and west, north and south. That being said, it’s sister airport, Dubai World Central, under the same Dubai Airports organization, is poised to surpass these feats by becoming the world’s largest global gateway with capacity of more than 160 million passengers per year and a multi-modal logistics hub for 12 million tonnes of air cargo. Since the commencement of its operations, the airport has already moved up to the 29th busiest air cargo airport in the world handling almost 760,000 metric tonnes of cargo in 2014. With its astonishing capacity and growth, aviation’s nucleus certainly has moved eastward.”

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

For consistency, the [Airports Council International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_Council_International "Airports Council International")'s (ACI) annual figures are always used in the final presentation and ranking, even where figures given by airport operators or authorities differ.

This article is about the busiest airports by passenger traffic. For the busiest airports in the world by international passenger traffic, see [List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic "List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic"). For the busiest cities by passenger traffic, see [List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_(cropped).jpg)

[Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport") in the [Atlanta metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Atlanta "Metro Atlanta"), the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic as of 2025

The world's busiest airport is [Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport") in [metropolitan Atlanta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Atlanta "Metro Atlanta"), which has been the world's busiest airport every year since 1998 with the exception of 2020, when its passenger traffic dipped for a year due to travel restrictions resulting from the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_commercial_air_transport "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on commercial air transport").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-1) Atlanta regained the top position in 2021,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-PANYNJ_2021_report-3) and has held it since. Alternatively, London has the [world's busiest city airport system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic") by passenger count.

As of 2025, the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") has the most airports in the top 50 list, with 14 (15 in 2024), followed by [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") with 12 (same as in 2024), while [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") each have two. In terms of regions, [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America") has 15 airports in the top 50 (17 in 2024), along with [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia") also with 15 (14 in 2024), [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") with eight (same as in 2024), [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") with five (same as in 2024), [West Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Asia "West Asia") with four (three in 2024), [South Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") with two (same as 2024), and [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America") with one (same as 2024).

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

For consistency, the [Airports Council International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_Council_International "Airports Council International")'s (ACI) annual figures are always used in the final presentation and ranking, even where figures given by airport operators or authorities differ.

This article is about the busiest airports by passenger traffic. For the busiest airports in the world by international passenger traffic, see [List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic "List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic"). For the busiest cities by passenger traffic, see [List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlanta_Hartsfield-Jackson_(cropped).jpg)

[Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport") in the [Atlanta metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Atlanta "Metro Atlanta"), the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic as of 2025

The world's busiest airport is [Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport") in [metropolitan Atlanta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Atlanta "Metro Atlanta"), which has been the world's busiest airport every year since 1998 with the exception of 2020, when its passenger traffic dipped for a year due to travel restrictions resulting from the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_on_commercial_air_transport "Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on commercial air transport").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-1) Atlanta regained the top position in 2021,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic#cite_note-PANYNJ_2021_report-3) and has held it since. Alternatively, London has the [world's busiest city airport system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic") by passenger count.

As of 2025, the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") has the most airports in the top 50 list, with 14 (15 in 2024), followed by [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") with 12 (same as in 2024), while [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") each have two. In terms of regions, [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America") has 15 airports in the top 50 (17 in 2024), along with [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia") also with 15 (14 in 2024), [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") with eight (same as in 2024), [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") with five (same as in 2024), [West Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Asia "West Asia") with four (three in 2024), [South Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") with two (same as 2024), and [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America") with one (same as 2024).

Top 30 world's busiest airports by international passenger traffic and top 50 world's busiest airports by passenger traffic. Data are measured by total passengers (data from Airports Council International (ACI), defined as passengers enplaned plus passengers deplaned plus direct-transit passengers. Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport in Atlanta has been the world's busiest airport every year since 2000; with all airports combined London has the world's busiest city airport system by passenger count. For a complete list of UK airports, see [List of airports in the United Kingdom and the British Crown Dependencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom_and_the_British_Crown_Dependencies "List of airports in the United Kingdom and the British Crown Dependencies").

The United Kingdom, an [island country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_country "Island country"), is home to many of Europe's largest and busiest airports. [London Heathrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport"), which handles over 83 million passengers annually, is the largest airport in the UK. London serves as the largest aviation hub in the world by passenger traffic, with six [international airports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_airport "International airport"), handling over 177 million passengers in 2024,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-caa2024-1) more than any other city ([List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic")). London's second-busiest airport, [London Gatwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Airport "Gatwick Airport"), was until 2016 the world's busiest single-runway airport.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-2)[Manchester Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Airport "Manchester Airport") is the United Kingdom's third-busiest airport. [London Stansted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stansted_Airport "Stansted Airport") and [London Luton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luton_Airport "Luton Airport") are the fourth and fifth busiest airports, respectively.

The largest airport operator in the United Kingdom is [Heathrow Airport Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport_Holdings "Heathrow Airport Holdings") (owner of Heathrow), followed by [Manchester Airports Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Airports_Group "Manchester Airports Group") (owner of Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands). Together with [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") and [Virgin Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Atlantic "Virgin Atlantic"), they are part of the Aviation Foundation which lobby for the aviation needs of the United Kingdom.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-3)

Although the top ten airports remained unchanged, the most notable shift was Liverpool John Lennon Airport overtaking Newcastle International Airport to claim eleventh place. This is a list of the **busiest airports in the United Kingdom, [Channel Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_Islands "Channel Islands"), and [Isle of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Man "Isle of Man") ranked by total passenger traffic**, compiled from [Civil Aviation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Aviation_Authority_(United_Kingdom) "Civil Aviation Authority (United Kingdom)") data from 2006 to 2024. For some years the figures also show total [aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft "Aircraft") movements and [cargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cargo "Cargo") volume handled at each airport. For a complete list of UK airports, see [List of airports in the United Kingdom and the British Crown Dependencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom_and_the_British_Crown_Dependencies "List of airports in the United Kingdom and the British Crown Dependencies").

The United Kingdom, an [island country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_country "Island country"), is home to many of Europe's largest and busiest airports. [London Heathrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport"), which handles over 83 million passengers annually, is the largest airport in the UK. London serves as the largest aviation hub in the world by passenger traffic, with six [international airports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_airport "International airport"), handling over 177 million passengers in 2024,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-caa2024-1) more than any other city ([List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest city airport systems by passenger traffic")). London's second-busiest airport, [London Gatwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Airport "Gatwick Airport"), was until 2016 the world's busiest single-runway airport.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-2)[Manchester Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Airport "Manchester Airport") is the United Kingdom's third-busiest airport. [London Stansted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stansted_Airport "Stansted Airport") and [London Luton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luton_Airport "Luton Airport") are the fourth and fifth busiest airports, respectively.

The largest airport operator in the United Kingdom is [Heathrow Airport Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport_Holdings "Heathrow Airport Holdings") (owner of Heathrow), followed by [Manchester Airports Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Airports_Group "Manchester Airports Group") (owner of Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands). Together with [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") and [Virgin Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Atlantic "Virgin Atlantic"), they are part of the Aviation Foundation which lobby for the aviation needs of the United Kingdom.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-3)

### 2024/2025 data

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_busiest_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 2024/2025 data")]

The following is a list of the 40 largest UK airports by total passenger traffic in 2025, from UK CAA statistics.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-:0-4)

Although the top ten airports remained unchanged, the most notable shift was Liverpool John Lennon Airport overtaking Newcastle International Airport to claim eleventh place. Another striking fact is the decline in passenger numbers at London Gatwick and Belfast International Airports, the second and tenth busiest UK airports respectively, despite a significant overall increase in passenger journeys, from 295 million in 2024 to 302 million in 2025.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_in_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-5)

Initially most change was experienced within the airline sector as a consequence o airline deregulation, privatisa-tion and globalisation trends. The pace o change was slower in the airport industry, but now this sector, too, has developed into a undamentally dierent business. The trend towards airline deregulation began in 1978 with the deregulation o the US domestic market. Many more markets were subsequently liberalised or deregulated, initially as the result o the adoption o more liberal bilateral air service agreements. In the European Union (EU), deregulation was achieved with a multilateral policy that evolved over a number o years with the introduction o the three deregulation packages in 1987, 1990 and 1993. The 1993 package, which did not become ully operational until 1997, was the most signicant and had the most ar-reaching impact. This European deregulation allowed a large low-cost carrier (LCC) industry to develop, which has had major conse-quences or many airports. This deregulation trend has continued in other parts o the world, a very signicant milestone being the introduction o the EU–US open aviation area in 2008.

These services include air trac control (ATC), security, and re and rescue in the aireld. Airports also oer a wide variety o com-mercial acilities ranging rom shops and restaurants to hotels, conerence services and business parks.As well as playing a crucial role within the air transport sector, airports have a strategic importance to the regions they serve. In addition, the Middle East area has seen very signicant increases in trac volumes, particular at Dubai airport, which handled over 84 million passengers in 2016 compared with ewer than 30 million in 2006.The growth in demand or air transport has had very signicant economic and envi-ronmental consequences or both the airline and airport industries. Moreover, since the 1970s there have been major regulatory and structural developments, which have pro-oundly aected the way in which the two industries operate. Initially most change was experienced within the airline sector as a consequence o airline deregulation, privatisa-tion and globalisation trends. The pace o change was slower in the airport industry, but now this sector, too, has developed into a undamentally dierent business. The trend towards airline deregulation began in 1978 with the deregulation o the US domestic market. Many more markets were subsequently liberalised or deregulated, initially as the result o the adoption o more liberal bilateral air service agreements. In the European Union (EU), deregulation was achieved with a multilateral policy that evolved over a number o years with the introduction o the three deregulation packages in 1987, 1990 and 1993. The 1993 package, which did not become ully operational until 1997, was the most signicant and had the most ar-reaching impact. This European deregulation allowed a large low-cost carrier (LCC) industry to develop, which has had major conse-quences or many airports. This deregulation trend has continued in other parts o the world, a very signicant milestone being the introduction o the EU–US open aviation area in 2008.

Land in Orlando, and the airport is built to push you out into the city as fast as possible. Land in Dubai, and you enter a captive ecosystem designed so you never actually leave.

The distinction between a destination airport and an international hub comes down to how they handle the flow of people and luggage. Destination airports prioritize "landside" infrastructure—massive baggage claims, sprawling rental car centers, and high-capacity access roads designed to funnel travelers into the local economy as quickly as possible.

True international hubs prioritize "airside" infrastructure. They invest heavily in sterile transit zones where passengers can move between gates without ever clearing local customs or securing transit visas. Behind the scenes, hubs rely on sophisticated underground baggage sorting systems that can instantly route a suitcase from an arriving Boeing 777 to a departing Airbus A380 on the opposite side of the airfield.

An airport cannot become a hub without a dominant anchor airline to orchestrate this flow. Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson routinely ranks as the world's busiest airport not because Atlanta is the world's most popular tourist destination, but because Delta Air Lines uses it as the geographic center of its route network. The airport's flight schedule is synchronized into distinct "banks," with dozens of incoming flights landing simultaneously, followed by a frantic two-hour window of passenger and baggage transfers, and then a coordinated wave of departures.

International hubs also exploit their exact geographic coordinates. Dubai sits within an eight-hour flight of two-thirds of the global population, making it an ideal midpoint for passengers traveling between Europe, Asia, and Australia on Emirates. Because hub passengers remain on airport property for hours between flights, these terminals function as self-contained miniature cities. To compete for layover traffic, premier hubs have escalated their airside amenities far beyond typical seating areas. Singapore Changi Airport routes its terminal-connecting Skytrain directly past a 130-foot indoor waterfall, transforming the otherwise tedious process of moving between gates into an architectural spectacle.

Slept all night, Wake, shower, dress and off the train in the middle of Sydney with a hour + to spare before my client arrived at work. Light breakfast. I felt GOOD and SHARP. All went well.

I thought ‘This is the way.’ Fare was much lower than air, AND overnight accomodation thrown in.

Next visit April 6th to Sydney approaching. So, Friday, I phoned the railway. ‘I need a sleeper to Sydney Tuesday, return Friday’.

‘What date?’ he asks.

‘The 6th.’. I reply ‘Return evening of 9th’.

Nice friendly chap, but I can almost hear him, bursting into laughter, calling his workmates ‘Hey! come and listen to this bloke’.

‘Lets see. Tuesday…. First available Tuesday is May 26th. Return on a Friday, ——- I’ve got two cancellations June 30th. Do you want me to book one of them?’

I'll take a stab at this, but others may have more insight. The bottom line is that airlines want to get all of the passengers they can at the lowest possible cost. Crudely, it's all about getting asses on seats. So, how to do that?

One approach is to focus your assets (aircraft and staff) in a few key markets, as Jet Blue did, by offering competitive fares, but only between cities with lots of passengers. That strategy is good in terms of cost per passenger, but misses many potential passengers in smaller markets. In a major metropolitan area with multiple airports airlines have the option of concentration or dispersion. It's more efficient to focus on one airport and make the passengers come to you; but if your competitors serve other airports, they could take “your” passengers.

Serving smaller cities allows an airline to capture more potential passengers, but increases the cost per passenger because, even though airport costs are a relatively small part of an airline's costs, it is still a cost. More importantly, serving many airports requires more aircraft and crews. Airlines address those issues in several ways. Given the smaller passenger volumes at smaller airports, airlines can employ smaller aircraft (typically operated by affiliated lower cost regional carriers). Alternatively, an airline could operate fewer flights, although operating a station at an airport requires a certain minimum amount of service to be worthwhile.

Many airlines serve smaller airports using the hub and spoke system. (Southwest uses a focus city concept, which has some of the characteristics of the hub and spoke system.) In the hub and spoke system smaller airports connect to hubs, where passengers not going to that city connect to flights to (hopefully) their desired destinations. Service to the spoke cities could be provided by a few mainline flights or by, posibility, more frequent service by regional carriers.

The main advantage to a small local airport are the lines are much shorter. I used to live in Pasadena Texas, on the east side of Houston. Continental Airlines used to run a “shuttle flight”, where I could check in at Ellington Field and fly to Bush Intercontinental or Hobby airports. The disadvantages are the added complexity and cost when planning a trip. For example, a flights from Boise Idaho mostly travel to airline hub cities. There are frequent flights to Seattle, Salt Lake. Denver and San Francisco. There might be a morning and evening flight to Las Vegas. This acceptable if you are planning a trip to Seattle, Salt Lake, Denver or San Francisco. It I want to fly to someplace else, like Chicago, Dallas, or Orlando, then I have to plan on layovers, where I might have to change planes and wait for the next flight.

Land in Orlando, and the airport is built to push you out into the city as fast as possible. Land in Dubai, and you enter a captive ecosystem designed so you never actually leave.

The distinction between a destination airport and an international hub comes down to how they handle the flow of people and luggage. Destination airports prioritize "landside" infrastructure—massive baggage claims, sprawling rental car centers, and high-capacity access roads designed to funnel travelers into the local economy as quickly as possible.

True international hubs prioritize "airside" infrastructure. They invest heavily in sterile transit zones where passengers can move between gates without ever clearing local customs or securing transit visas. Behind the scenes, hubs rely on sophisticated underground baggage sorting systems that can instantly route a suitcase from an arriving Boeing 777 to a departing Airbus A380 on the opposite side of the airfield.

An airport cannot become a hub without a dominant anchor airline to orchestrate this flow. Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson routinely ranks as the world's busiest airport not because Atlanta is the world's most popular tourist destination, but because Delta Air Lines uses it as the geographic center of its route network. The airport's flight schedule is synchronized into distinct "banks," with dozens of incoming flights landing simultaneously, followed by a frantic two-hour window of passenger and baggage transfers, and then a coordinated wave of departures.

International hubs also exploit their exact geographic coordinates. Dubai sits within an eight-hour flight of two-thirds of the global population, making it an ideal midpoint for passengers traveling between Europe, Asia, and Australia on Emirates. Because hub passengers remain on airport property for hours between flights, these terminals function as self-contained miniature cities. To compete for layover traffic, premier hubs have escalated their airside amenities far beyond typical seating areas. Singapore Changi Airport routes its terminal-connecting Skytrain directly past a 130-foot indoor waterfall, transforming the otherwise tedious process of moving between gates into an architectural spectacle.

I was at a race meeting with my father in Brisbane when I was about 14 y/o. the track is adjacent to the airport and it was announced the 3:15 race was being delayed because the the flight from Sydney (Saturday & Wednesday) was about to arrive (late).

This was 1953 (give or take a year). Originally from Sydney, we spent most school holidays there and caught the train or drove. (That’s another story.) The train was overnight. Also for Navy (reserve) training later on.

1,000 years later (1966 on) I flew to Sydney (rtn) regularly on business. Either late afternoon and stay in an hotel OR, far too early for humans, in the morning.

Then one evening, some business emergency, when I was in Lismore N.S.W. the only option was to catch the train from Kyogle (one of the three stops on the Bris/Syd route). Lucky there was a share sleeper cancellation.

Slept all night, Wake, shower, dress and off the train in the middle of Sydney with a hour + to spare before my client arrived at work. Light breakfast. I felt GOOD and SHARP. All went well.

I thought ‘This is the way.’ Fare was much lower than air, AND overnight accomodation thrown in.

Next visit April 6th to Sydney approaching. So, Friday, I phoned the railway. ‘I need a sleeper to Sydney Tuesday, return Friday’.

‘What date?’ he asks.

‘The 6th.’. I reply ‘Return evening of 9th’.

Nice friendly chap, but I can almost hear him, bursting into laughter, calling his workmates ‘Hey! come and listen to this bloke’.

‘Lets see. Tuesday…. First available Tuesday is May 26th. Return on a Friday, ——- I’ve got two cancellations June 30th. Do you want me to book one of them?’

For Business, there are about 5 or 6 flights per hour between 6:00 a.m. and 9:00p.m. I can phone and be in the air within an hour. A ‘faster’ train each hour, in the evening, depart 5:00//6:00//7:00 and arriving between 6:00 and 9:00 in the morning would pull a lot of commercial trade. Dinner, a few drinks, Good sleep. Shower and dress. Much better than squeezy or a Kings ransom in a plane.

Flying to Townsville or Cairns N.Q. I loved the Fokker Friendship ‘Daylight Milk run’ flights. Low and slow along the coast out over the Great Barrier Reef. BIG windows High wings that didn’t block the view. Real tourist stuff. Spectacular. I’ve driven that route a lot but never taken the train.

I'll take a stab at this, but others may have more insight. The bottom line is that airlines want to get all of the passengers they can at the lowest possible cost. Crudely, it's all about getting asses on seats. So, how to do that?

One approach is to focus your assets (aircraft and staff) in a few key markets, as Jet Blue did, by offering competitive fares, but only between cities with lots of passengers. That strategy is good in terms of cost per passenger, but misses many potential passengers in smaller markets. In a major metropolitan area with multiple airports airlines have the option of concentration or dispersion. It's more efficient to focus on one airport and make the passengers come to you; but if your competitors serve other airports, they could take “your” passengers.

Serving smaller cities allows an airline to capture more potential passengers, but increases the cost per passenger because, even though airport costs are a relatively small part of an airline's costs, it is still a cost. More importantly, serving many airports requires more aircraft and crews. Airlines address those issues in several ways. Given the smaller passenger volumes at smaller airports, airlines can employ smaller aircraft (typically operated by affiliated lower cost regional carriers). Alternatively, an airline could operate fewer flights, although operating a station at an airport requires a certain minimum amount of service to be worthwhile.

Many airlines serve smaller airports using the hub and spoke system. (Southwest uses a focus city concept, which has some of the characteristics of the hub and spoke system.) In the hub and spoke system smaller airports connect to hubs, where passengers not going to that city connect to flights to (hopefully) their desired destinations. Service to the spoke cities could be provided by a few mainline flights or by, posibility, more frequent service by regional carriers.

## Abstract

Airports are of particular significance for contemporary cities. They are not just places where airplanes take off and land, but also hubs where locality combines with globality. The transport hubs have always played an important role in city development. Harbors, railway stations or major crossroads were the locations of intense contacts, it was here that settlement structures developed. As privileged locations, they attracted investments and became economic growth centres. A similar phenomenon can be observed for airports. As the number of the transported passengers and goods grows, the terminals develop additional functions. Airport-proximate zones are prestigious sites with good traffic connections. Investment accumulation based on the snow-ball effect results in creating new building complexes, called Airport City. Those are sites where the flow of people, goods and capital takes place and which are the focal points of the urbanization processes in the global economy. But can the Airport City be compared to a city as a shopping gallery to a gallery or an industrial park to a park? Can urban space be created there and if so, what type of city is it?

3.   Investments in airport zones are driven by increased passenger traffic, leading to multifunctional urban areas.
4.   'Aerotropolis' is a model for airport-related urban regions, distinguishing them from traditional urban spaces.
5.   Future trends include sustainable airport designs, advanced transportation, and enhanced passenger experiences through technology.

Airports have been relatively neglected in scholarly planning literature despite their historic role in shaping metropolitan form. Reviewing the trends and planning issues arising, several normative models of airport spaces are identified and discussed in relation to sustainable development objectives. The contestation of airport expansion that has made for epic political battles in diverse settings and its implications for models of airport-led urban development is noted. Considering the crucial role of airports in the 21st-century globalized world; travel activities such as international connections, business contacts, congresses, accommodation, and so forth should take place in a short time with easy access. Airport cities can provide all these elements without the need to go to the metropolitan city center and generate a new potential for the reconstruction and development of metropolitan areas. This study aims to investigate the basic information about airport cities with their spatial structure, components, general characteristics, environmental and economic impacts, and critical contributions to metropolitan areas through a theoretical framework. The study consists of three main stages in the framework of qualitative methods, such as data collection, comparison, and evaluation: (I) introduction and theoretical investigation of airport cities with their historical background, key concepts and characteristics, effects on the environment, and their role in sustainability; (II) inquiry into the theoretical knowledge through a case study (Stockholm–Arlanda Airport City); (III) and discussions on the potentials, possible impacts, and stimulating dynamics of airport cities regarding the future of metropolitan areas.

The increasing volume of air travel and freight has led scholars to ponder the possibility of an aerotropolis, or airport city. Proponents of the aerotropolis argue that future cities will develop around airports, just as contemporary cities are organized around other means of transport such as train stations. However, critics do not agree with such a futuristic vision. Despite ongoing debates regarding the aerotropolis model, the increasing importance of airport-related infrastructures is illustrated by the recent enlargements of airports. This article considers the case of South Korea's Songdo International City in order to discuss the architectural aesthetics of the airport city generally. The author first traces accounts of both real and imagined airport cities in architectural and planning literature. She then proceeds to analyze the case study site as an example of the role of architecture in shaping public space. While most discussions of the airport city idea seem to suggest the existence of boundless opportunities, the task of balancing the development needs for urban infrastructure and for housing has eluded the current governance system based on the private-public partnership. Further discussions are needed on how to balance mobile and place-based activities so as to make airport cities livable.

Cities grow and prosper in relation with their transportation hubs. In the past, coastal towns with adequate harbors grew and expanded quickly. In modern times, similar prospects apply to cities with airports which provide competitive advantages for regional and urban development. In addition to being a complex system of facilities, airports are significant stimulators for economic activities in its catchment area. In the last thirty years or so, airports have become clusters of not only transportation-related operational services but also commercial and business activities. Accordingly, airports have grown into complex and multi-faced mega structures, offering space for longer runways and larger terminals, and accommodating a growing number of functions that have nothing related with aviation. Hence, Aerotropolis defined by Prof. Dr. Kasarda is regarded as an urban cluster with similar features to the traditional metropolitan structure. In its core, Airport City is located which functions as the traditional city center of Aerotropolis. This thesis focuses on the principles and relationships for land use planning and design of airports and their environs under the umbrella of Airport City concept. It is aimed to underline current design framework of Airport Cities which is found missing in terms of academic studies. In this context, the Airport City model clarified, and selected cases have been evaluated under certain design principles in order to have an output about design criteria of the Airport City development. The research concludes with inferences regarding existing design guidelines of certain Airport City cases.

[Michal Stangel](https://politechnikaslaska.academia.edu/MichalStangel)

The notion of placemaking and sustainable urbanism praise dense, urban grids with unique public spaces. Airports, on the other hand, have been often criticized as model “non-places”– strange, anonymous spaces of transience that do not hold enough spatial significance. From this perspective at airport-related areas one may ask, in fact, how urban may they become, and weather the "Airport City" has more in common with the city than a "shopping gallery" to an art gallery, or than a "business park" to a park? While the spatial configuration of the commercial functions surrounding the airport terminal have resembled those of a large shopping malls, or suburban commercial zones, with freestanding objects separated by parking lots, the airport cities currently designed are envisioned as dense, multifunctional urban districts. Recent projects, such as the Airport Cities in Warsaw, Stockholm, Manchester etc. elaborate on qualities such as carefully designed open spaces, iconic architecture and public art. In this perspective, sustainable airport districts shall be development with rational use of resources and maximizing social, economic and environmental benefits. Within the paradigm of sustainable urbanism, this would mean a holistic approach in three scales: developing specific districts in polycentric metropolises, shaping their urban structure, and designing specific places within the scale of urban blocks.

## Abstract

Airports are of particular significance for contemporary cities. They are not just places where airplanes take off and land, but also hubs where locality combines with globality. The transport hubs have always played an important role in city development. Harbors, railway stations or major crossroads were the locations of intense contacts, it was here that settlement structures developed. As privileged locations, they attracted investments and became economic growth centres. A similar phenomenon can be observed for airports. As the number of the transported passengers and goods grows, the terminals develop additional functions. Airport-proximate zones are prestigious sites with good traffic connections. Investment accumulation based on the snow-ball effect results in creating new building complexes, called Airport City. Those are sites where the flow of people, goods and capital takes place and which are the focal points of the urbanization processes in the global economy. But can the Airport City be compared to a city as a shopping gallery to a gallery or an industrial park to a park? Can urban space be created there and if so, what type of city is it?

Airports have been relatively neglected in scholarly planning literature despite their historic role in shaping metropolitan form. Reviewing the trends and planning issues arising, several normative models of airport spaces are identified and discussed in relation to sustainable development objectives. The contestation of airport expansion that has made for epic political battles in diverse settings and its implications for models of airport-led urban development is noted. Airport cities could be defined as examples of postmodern cities in metropolitan areas in which the airport (with its related departments) is centered as a focal point and other facilities encircle the airport hub up to 30 kms outward in a mutualistic manner. Considering the crucial role of airports in the 21st-century globalized world; travel activities such as international connections, business contacts, congresses, accommodation, and so forth should take place in a short time with easy access. Airport cities can provide all these elements without the need to go to the metropolitan city center and generate a new potential for the reconstruction and development of metropolitan areas. This study aims to investigate the basic information about airport cities with their spatial structure, components, general characteristics, environmental and economic impacts, and critical contributions to metropolitan areas through a theoretical framework. The study consists of three main stages in the framework of qualitative methods, such as data collection, comparison, and evaluation: (I) introduction and theoretical investigation of airport cities with their historical background, key concepts and characteristics, effects on the environment, and their role in sustainability; (II) inquiry into the theoretical knowledge through a case study (Stockholm–Arlanda Airport City); (III) and discussions on the potentials, possible impacts, and stimulating dynamics of airport cities regarding the future of metropolitan areas.

The increasing volume of air travel and freight has led scholars to ponder the possibility of an aerotropolis, or airport city. Proponents of the aerotropolis argue that future cities will develop around airports, just as contemporary cities are organized around other means of transport such as train stations. However, critics do not agree with such a futuristic vision. Despite ongoing debates regarding the aerotropolis model, the increasing importance of airport-related infrastructures is illustrated by the recent enlargements of airports. This article considers the case of South Korea's Songdo International City in order to discuss the architectural aesthetics of the airport city generally. The author first traces accounts of both real and imagined airport cities in architectural and planning literature. She then proceeds to analyze the case study site as an example of the role of architecture in shaping public space. While most discussions of the airport city idea seem to suggest the existence of boundless opportunities, the task of balancing the development needs for urban infrastructure and for housing has eluded the current governance system based on the private-public partnership. Further discussions are needed on how to balance mobile and place-based activities so as to make airport cities livable.

Cities grow and prosper in relation with their transportation hubs. In the past, coastal towns with adequate harbors grew and expanded quickly. In modern times, similar prospects apply to cities with airports which provide competitive advantages for regional and urban development. In addition to being a complex system of facilities, airports are significant stimulators for economic activities in its catchment area. In the last thirty years or so, airports have become clusters of not only transportation-related operational services but also commercial and business activities. Accordingly, airports have grown into complex and multi-faced mega structures, offering space for longer runways and larger terminals, and accommodating a growing number of functions that have nothing related with aviation. Hence, Aerotropolis defined by Prof. Dr. Kasarda is regarded as an urban cluster with similar features to the traditional metropolitan structure. In its core, Airport City is located which functions as the traditional city center of Aerotropolis. This thesis focuses on the principles and relationships for land use planning and design of airports and their environs under the umbrella of Airport City concept. It is aimed to underline current design framework of Airport Cities which is found missing in terms of academic studies. In this context, the Airport City model clarified, and selected cases have been evaluated under certain design principles in order to have an output about design criteria of the Airport City development. The research concludes with inferences regarding existing design guidelines of certain Airport City cases.

[Michal Stangel](https://politechnikaslaska.academia.edu/MichalStangel)

The notion of placemaking and sustainable urbanism praise dense, urban grids with unique public spaces. Airports, on the other hand, have been often criticized as model “non-places”– strange, anonymous spaces of transience that do not hold enough spatial significance. From this perspective at airport-related areas one may ask, in fact, how urban may they become, and weather the "Airport City" has more in common with the city than a "shopping gallery" to an art gallery, or than a "business park" to a park? While the spatial configuration of the commercial functions surrounding the airport terminal have resembled those of a large shopping malls, or suburban commercial zones, with freestanding objects separated by parking lots, the airport cities currently designed are envisioned as dense, multifunctional urban districts. Recent projects, such as the Airport Cities in Warsaw, Stockholm, Manchester etc. elaborate on qualities such as carefully designed open spaces, iconic architecture and public art. In this perspective, sustainable airport districts shall be development with rational use of resources and maximizing social, economic and environmental benefits. Within the paradigm of sustainable urbanism, this would mean a holistic approach in three scales: developing specific districts in polycentric metropolises, shaping their urban structure, and designing specific places within the scale of urban blocks.

Most likely answer: Atlanta Hartsfield–Jackson (ATL).

Supporting points:

*   ATL has been the world’s busiest airport by passenger numbers for many years, handling the largest number of connecting passengers in the U.S. Its geography (southeast U.S. location) and Delta Air Lines’ hub operations create extremely high transfer volumes between domestic and international flights.
*   Characteristics that make an airport a heavy connector hub: very high total enplanements, a dominant network carrier using the airport as a primary hub, high percentage of connecting (vs. origin/destination) passengers, and schedule banks that concentrate arrivals and departures. ATL scores highly on all these metrics.
*   Other major U.S. connecting hubs (but less so than ATL): Chicago O’Hare (ORD), Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW), Denver (DEN), and Charlotte (CLT). Each is a primary interchange for their main carriers (United at ORD, American at DFW and CLT, United at DEN) and handles many connections, but overall connecting-passenger share and absolute numbers historically remain below ATL.

Data context:

*   Traffic patterns and airline network structures through May 2024 continue to show ATL leading in total passengers and transfer volumes; individual years and seasonal schedules can shift relative rankings, but ATL consistently functions as the principal U.S. connecting airport.

Since you specifically mention people this may not be the specific answer you’re looking for, but if you’re just looking for America’s biggest hub airports, they’re located in Memphis and Louisville. Why haven’t you ever changed planes there? Because most of their traffic is cargo.

Memphis: The primary hub of FedEx Express.

![Image 12](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-029993a8ffb7e6c3768d9c9f26945e59-lq)

See how many routes land in Memphis? And those are just the international routes. The domestic routes are even busier. FedEx doesn’t publish many specifics on their operations out of Memphis but the Wikipedia page for Memphis International Airport liste hundreds of destinations for FedEx Express flights out of Memphis.

Louisville: Louisville International Airport hosts the UPS Worldport. UPS doesn’t seem to publish route maps like FedEx, but Wikipedia says: “Louisville International Airport (Standiford Field)in Louisville, Kentucky, the primary hub of UPS Airlines, and home to Worldport and the corporate headquarters of UPS Airlines. With approximately 251 inbound and outbound flights daily, the service area for Worldport is over 200 countries worldwide. Approximately each hour, the facility handles 416,000 individual packages. Along with the 5.2 million square foot Worldport facility, UPS also operates a 654,000 square foot freight facility at the airport”

Louisville and Memphis don’t handle as many passengers as other airports, but based on sheer payload weight (be it human or freight) that uses the airport as a hub, these two airports almost certainly win the title of biggest hubs. Unlike the passenger airlines, the freight carriers have made no attempt to move away from the hub and spoke model. It seems to work better for freight than for people.

Freight also complains a lot less and doesn’t care if the cabin is a little cold.

Most likely answer: Atlanta Hartsfield–Jackson (ATL).

Supporting points:

*   ATL has been the world’s busiest airport by passenger numbers for many years, handling the largest number of connecting passengers in the U.S. Its geography (southeast U.S. location) and Delta Air Lines’ hub operations create extremely high transfer volumes between domestic and international flights.
*   Characteristics that make an airport a heavy connector hub: very high total enplanements, a dominant network carrier using the airport as a primary hub, high percentage of connecting (vs. origin/destination) passengers, and schedule banks that concentrate arrivals and departures. ATL scores highly on all these metrics.
*   Other major U.S. connecting hubs (but less so than ATL): Chicago O’Hare (ORD), Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW), Denver (DEN), and Charlotte (CLT). Each is a primary interchange for their main carriers (United at ORD, American at DFW and CLT, United at DEN) and handles many connections, but overall connecting-passenger share and absolute numbers historically remain below ATL.

Data context:

*   Traffic patterns and airline network structures through May 2024 continue to show ATL leading in total passengers and transfer volumes; individual years and seasonal schedules can shift relative rankings, but ATL consistently functions as the principal U.S. connecting airport.

Since you specifically mention people this may not be the specific answer you’re looking for, but if you’re just looking for America’s biggest hub airports, they’re located in Memphis and Louisville. Why haven’t you ever changed planes there? Because most of their traffic is cargo.

Memphis: The primary hub of FedEx Express.

![Image 12](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-029993a8ffb7e6c3768d9c9f26945e59-lq)

See how many routes land in Memphis? And those are just the international routes. The domestic routes are even busier. FedEx doesn’t publish many specifics on their operations out of Memphis but the Wikipedia page for Memphis International Airport liste hundreds of destinations for FedEx Express flights out of Memphis.

Louisville: Louisville International Airport hosts the UPS Worldport. UPS doesn’t seem to publish route maps like FedEx, but Wikipedia says: “Louisville International Airport (Standiford Field)in Louisville, Kentucky, the primary hub of UPS Airlines, and home to Worldport and the corporate headquarters of UPS Airlines. With approximately 251 inbound and outbound flights daily, the service area for Worldport is over 200 countries worldwide. Approximately each hour, the facility handles 416,000 individual packages. Along with the 5.2 million square foot Worldport facility, UPS also operates a 654,000 square foot freight facility at the airport”

Louisville and Memphis don’t handle as many passengers as other airports, but based on sheer payload weight (be it human or freight) that uses the airport as a hub, these two airports almost certainly win the title of biggest hubs. Unlike the passenger airlines, the freight carriers have made no attempt to move away from the hub and spoke model. It seems to work better for freight than for people.

Freight also complains a lot less and doesn’t care if the cabin is a little cold.

These are the busiest airports worldwide

The world’s busiest airports would likely be major hubs with travellers from around the globe. Usually, this would make these giants a sort of anthropological gems, places where the modern world meets.

So which are the biggest airports by passenger movements?

1.   Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) Hartsfield- Jackson has been the world’s biggest airport by passenger traffic since 2000. Its business has only grown since then. As of 2018, more than 107 million passengers arrive or depart from Atlanta International Airport each year. This means that the airport accommodates nearly 295,000 passengers daily. The airport offers services to both domestic and international destinations in five different continents: North America, South America, Europe, Africa and Asia. Hartsfield-Jackson Airport serves as the main hub of Delta Air Lines and 72% of its flights are operated by Delta.

Beijing Capital International Airport (PEK) Beijing Capital opened in the 1950s but only in the last decade, it has risen to one of the biggest airports in the world in terms of number of passengers. In 2017 alone, passenger traffic exceeded 95 million. It is a hub for China’s major airlines: Air China, China Eastern and China Southern Airlines, as well as Hainan. Beijing Capital has become an important meeting point of Asia, Europe and North America. Nevertheless, the airport has retained its Chinese roots. Passengers can walk through miniature imperial architecture with gardens and bridges imitating Beijing’s famous Summer Palace. Travellers with a longer layover can also pay a short trip to the Great Wall of China. In case there’s not enough time for that, you may still enjoy your time at the airport. As one of the largest airports in the world and a major world hub, BCIA offers more than 70 different restaurants with food from around the globe. In addition, the airport has more than four football fields of area with retail and services options.

1.   Dubai International Airport (DXB)  
If we were ranking the world’s largest airports by international flight traffic, Dubai International Airport would have topped the list. It is the major transport hub in the middle east. However, due to the smaller number of domestic flights, this airport in the United Arab Emirates ranks as the third biggest airport in the world. Dubai International Airport is the main hub for the city’s two international carriers- Emirates and flydubai.   
Another 140 airlines operate flights to and from the airport. Hand in hand with Dubai’s increasing popularity in the last two decades, the airport’s growth passenger traffic has been staggering. Passenger movements (arrivals and departures) have grown from 4 million to close to 90 million in 2018.   
When Terminal 3 was built, it became the largest building in the world by area. At the time of writing, this terminal of the airport covers only flights operated by Emirates and Qantas.   
Dubai International Airport contributes a staggering $27 billion to Dubai’s economy which equals close to 27% of its GDP. Aviation in Dubai also contributes to 21% of employment. In the next years, its significance is expected only to increase and to contribute to 35% of employment and to bring in $88 billion dollars.
2.   Los Angeles International Airport (LAX)  
LAX served more than 87 million passengers in 2018, which makes it the fourth busiest airport in the world. It comes second in the United States for passenger movements, according to Airports Council International.   
Los Angeles International is a major connection point for international flights, particularly to other countries in North America, South America and Asia.  
As it is by far the largest airport on the East Coast, it serves as a hub for all major US airlines.   
If you ever find yourself in the area, make sure to pronounce the letters of LAX separately. The airport’s designation used to be just LA until the 1930s. Aviation’s rapid growth, however, necessitated three-letter identifiers, so an “X” was added. In and of itself the “X” is meaningless.

It makes sense that the largest metropolitan area in the world would also house one of the busiest airports worldwide. In fact, despite an increase in passenger movements, it was recently surpassed by LAX as the fourth busiest airport. In 2018, it accommodated just over 87 million travelers.   
It is the major hub for Japan’s two biggest airlines: All Nippon Airways and Japan Airlines.   
Tokyo will host the 2020 Olympic Games and passengers should expect a further development of Tokyo Haneda, which will improve its connectivity.   
Few passengers would like to connect flights at one of the biggest world airports.   
But if you are connecting at Tokyo Haneda, make sure to stroll down Edo-koji street. The restaurants and shops there are designed to imitate traditional Japanese architecture and you can find fantastic food and memorable souvenirs to complete your trip to Japan.   
Tokyo Haneda was ranked #3 among world’s best airports in 2018 according to Skytrax. In addition, it was voted World’s Cleanest Airport and World’s Best Domestic Airport in 2018.

Chicago O’Hare was the most used airport in the world between 1963 and 1998. With 83 million passengers served in 2018, it was the sixth busiest airport globally.   
After becoming a symbol of the jet area in the 1960s and 1970s, America’s second largest airport continues to be a pioneer of innovations.   
It was the first airport in the world to host an apiary which became home to more than a million bees. The bees were kept by former convicts from the Chicago, Illinois area in a successful effort to teach the former prisoners new skills and help them become more employable.

It consists of four active terminals (T2-T5), with another to open if the third runway is built. Three of them are dedicated to the three major alliances, and Terminal 5 the national carrier: [British Airways](https://skyrefund.com/en/airlines/british-airways "skyrefund.com").   
It is a major hub for British Airways and to an extent Virgin Atlantic (mainly operating out of Gatwick).  
The most common international routes from LHR are to and from New York- JFK, Dubai International Airport and Dublin. As Europe’s busiest airport, Heathrow is expected to play a big part in the UK’s economy following Brexit.
6.   Hong Kong International Airport (HKG)

The airport is built on land reclaimed from the sea specifically for the construction of the airport. Furthermore, the expansion of the airport to include a third runway and an additional concourse has been agreed.   
HKG was ranked fourth by Skytrax in its best airports rankings. It is World’s Best Transit Airport and the Best Airport for Dining.   
Being one of the largest airports in the world has its perks. If you have a few hours to spend at Hong Kong Intl Airport, don’t miss playing a few holes of golf, or watching an IMAX movie. You can find both at Terminal 2.

Shanghai Pudong only entered the top 10 of the largest global airports in 2016. However, thanks to a growth rarely seen, it will likely remain amongst them for the foreseeable future.   
As of 2018, Shanghai Pudong served 74 million passengers on mostly international flights. The main reason behind this growth is the airport’s expansion, completed in 2015, which effectively doubled the airport’s capacity. Today, the airport has two terminals and five runways.   
And while Pudong’s passenger concourses may not be that impressive in and of themselves, you could take a maglev (magnetic levitation) train to the city and feel your heart rate rise as the train’s speed surpasses 430 km/h.   
We hope these super-high-speed trains will help more passengers in avoiding a missed flight.

Paris Charles de Gaulle, France’s largest airport, was built in an avant-garde style in the 1960s and 70s and consists of 3 terminals. I waited a few days from when this A2A appeared in my feed because I knew the answer was just about to change. However, there is a bit of controversy about how you count the size of these airports.

Many sources online, are out of date and quote the originally planned size, not the actual size of the building when complete, white are often different things. Also, newspapers tend to use woolly language like “almost”, “nearly” and “about”, rounding the number as convenient. Then someone else quoted them, and rounds the number again or “about” or “nearly” something else. Add to that, the fact that many of the claims of “largest” are made in the future tense without specifying when that future. The claims of future record size often do not take into account other projects also under construction. And, as if it isn’t complicated enough, These large construction projects are often built in phases. When the terminal or airport opens, the full construction might not have completed all the phases. The building might not yet be as big as some reports might make out.

So, let us try to cut through some of this mess and get some sort of picture of what is going on. Although it might not be clear which building is actually the biggest, all of the buildings discussed below are very big and all of them deserve to be ogled at by passengers for their size, modern technology, engineering, and architecture.

The brand new Beijing Daxing International Airport (PKX) in China claims to be the largest single-structure airport terminal in the world. It opened officially two days ago but the first commercial flight was just yesterday (26th September 2019).

![Image 9](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-4800ae583cd33216b7d2dd90358849d7-lq)

Above: Arial view of Beijing Daxing International Airport near the end of construction.

The terminal building is haled by the media as the largest single-structure airport terminals in the world, with an area of more than 1,030,000 square metres for the main building and 1,430,000 square metres for the entire terminal complex. The terminal has 5 floors and 82 boarding gates. The construction used 220,000 tons of steel and came with a price tag of nearly US$14 billion.

Construction began in December 2014 and the building was designed by the architects ADP Ingenierie Architects (France) and Zaha Hadid Studios. The initial construction features 3 civilian runways (two North-South and one East-West) but it is planned to expand to 6 civilian runways plus 1 military runway, making a total of 7.

The plans for the expansion will also include a second terminal and island concourse south of the main terminal. It is expected that by 2025, the airport will be receiving over 72,000,000 passengers per year and it will have a capacity for 100,000,000, putting it among the busiest in the world.

![Image 10](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-3747dcc38fc4c47bff783736cfe5c8c6-lq)

Above: Inside Beijing Daxing International Airport

![Image 11](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-e867132671abd255059a9c7eabe0e093-lq)

Above: Beijing Capital International Airport T3, Beijing’s other airport.

Beijing Daxing International Airport will operate alongside Beijing Capital International Airport (PEK), located 65 km away, to the north-east of the Beijing city. The T3 of Beijing Capital International Airport briefly held the title of the largest airport terminal when it opened in 2008. It has a similar capacity to the new Daxing Airport but has been stretched right to its limits with 100,983,290 passengers passing through in 2018. Technically, Beijing Capital’s T3 isn’t one building, but 3 buildings, closely located and connected by a train. In total, T3 covers 986,000 square metres according to Wikipedia, however, Foster + Partners website, the architects who designed it, give a number of 1,300,000 square metres. So, depending on who you believe, it is a bit smaller, or a lot smaller, than the other airport terminals in this post which were all built after Beijing Capital International Airport T3 opened. It isn’t easy to find out the sizes of each of the three buildings of the terminal, but since T3C and T3E are about equal size, we might estimate that no one building can be more than 500,000 to 600,000 square metres.

![Image 12](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-84f064d1c34a42eaa538677ddc311582-lq)

Now, there is also Istanbul Airport which opened just last year, 29 October 2018. Its designers claimed it to be 1,440,000 square metres making it the largest single terminal building under a single roof.

Notice there is a bit of play on words going on here. Istanbul says “single roof” while Daxing uses “single-structure”. The full terminal structure of Daxing is cut by the access roads. The northern leg of the starfish-shaped terminal technically has a separate roof from the other six legs. However, even though it is two roofs, you don’t go outside to get from one leg to the other. Hence why Daxing is 1,030,000 square metres for the main building and 1,430,000 square metres for the entire terminal complex.

If you have been observant, you might notice that 1,440,000 square metres is more than 1,430,000 square metres. If those numbers are accurate, then that would mean that Istanbul is just a little bit bigger than Beijing Daxing. So why does Beijing claim to be the biggest?

What I think has happened, is that the claims of being the biggest date to when the first construction plans were being presented. When Beijing Daxing was under planning, it would have become the biggest if nobody else built something bigger in the meantime. So they were quite right to say that they were building what would become the biggest, based on what the existing competition was at that time.

Of course, in-between Beijing starting construction and the final opening date, Istanbul airport was completed. But journalists are sometimes lazy about checking facts. If someone else has made a certain claim, and another source repeated that claim, then that must be true, so let us just reprint that same claim without actually looking at the number.

So as it stands, unless someone has a different number of the size of these buildings, I would say that Istanbul beats Beijing Daxing, but only by a tiny bit.

![Image 13](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-82c011ede3525063e1f034eef9ce7604-lq)

Now, Wikipedia maintains a [list of largest buildings](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/List_of_largest_buildings "www.wikiwand.com"), and on that list, it puts Dubai International (DXB) Terminal 3 as the largest airport terminal in the world. It contains 1,713,000 square metres of space. However, like Beijing Capital, many would say that Dubai T3 is really multiple island concourse’s joined by tunnels. You can decide if you think that it that is one building, partially underground, or several buildings.

Now for a few honorary mentions.

![Image 15](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-d1057c9fdc0a7447affaf2512ffd8ec9-lq)

![Image 16](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-7b95a4b0a60902610b72be55a0810c67-lq)
